Prompt :
CREATE A PREMIUM, ULTRA-REALISTIC FEMALE CHARACTER
REFERENCE SHEET — CINEMATIC FILM PRODUCTION DESIGN
AND HIGH-END CHARACTER PORTFOLIO.

REFERENCE IMAGE / IDENTITY LOCK:
Use the uploaded reference image as the ONLY source
of the character's identity.

Preserve the exact facial identity, facial structure,
face shape, eyes, eyebrows, nose, lips, jawline,
skin tone, natural facial asymmetry, hairstyle,
hair color, hair texture, and overall appearance
from the reference image.

The character must remain the SAME PERSON in every
panel, angle, expression, outfit, and environment.

DO NOT redesign, beautify, age, de-age, or alter
the character's face.

Do not replace the face with a generic AI-generated
woman. Do not change ethnicity, facial proportions,
or recognizable identity.

Create a professional, production-ready character
reference sheet that looks like it was designed
for a high-budget cinematic film or premium streaming
series.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
CHARACTER DESIGN
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Create a believable female character based on the
uploaded reference image.

Use a realistic, natural human physique that matches
the reference image. Preserve the character's
approximate height, body proportions, and build.

Develop a sophisticated, realistic visual identity
without changing her core appearance.

The overall presentation should feel:
• Cinematic
• Premium
• Photorealistic
• Sophisticated
• Professional
• Natural
• Film-production ready

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
SHEET STRUCTURE & LAYOUT
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Create ONE complete, highly detailed character sheet
in a professional editorial grid layout.

Use a dark cinematic background with subtle charcoal,
black, warm gray, and muted neutral tones.

Include clean panel divisions, thin elegant borders,
balanced spacing, premium typography, and a coherent
visual hierarchy.

The layout must resemble a high-end film character
design portfolio, not a random collage.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
SECTION 1 — HERO PORTRAIT
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Place a large cinematic hero portrait in the upper-left
section.

Show the character in a natural, confident,
emotionally expressive pose.

Use realistic skin texture, natural lighting,
cinematic shadows, and premium photographic detail.

Add a handwritten-style character name and a short
character tagline.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
SECTION 2 — CHARACTER INFORMATION
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Place a clean character information panel beside
the hero portrait.

Include:

NAME: [GENERATE A SUITABLE CHARACTER NAME]
AGE: [SUITABLE AGE BASED ON THE CHARACTER]
NATIONALITY: [APPROPRIATE DESCRIPTION]
PROFESSION: [SUITABLE PROFESSION]
PERSONALITY: [3–5 CHARACTER TRAITS]
HEIGHT: [APPROXIMATE HEIGHT]
BUILD: [SLIM / ATHLETIC / AVERAGE / ETC.]
STYLE: [CHARACTER'S STYLE]
ROLE: [PROTAGONIST / SUPPORTING / ETC.]

Keep the information visually organized and easy
to read.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
SECTION 3 — FULL BODY TURNAROUND
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Create four consistent full-body views:

1. FRONT VIEW
2. BACK VIEW
3. LEFT PROFILE VIEW
4. RIGHT PROFILE VIEW

Maintain the EXACT SAME face, hairstyle, body,
clothing, proportions, and character identity
across all views.

Use a neutral studio background, consistent lighting,
and natural standing posture.

Clearly label each view.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Include realistic headshots showing:

• Front view
• Left profile
• Right profile
• Three-quarter left
• Three-quarter right
• Back of head

Preserve the character's exact facial identity,
hairstyle, hairline, and facial proportions.

Use consistent lighting and camera distance.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
SECTION 5 — FACIAL EXPRESSIONS
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Include a series of consistent facial expression
portraits:

• Neutral
• Happy
• Serious
• Sad
• Angry
• Thinking
• Confident

Expressions must look natural and believable.

Do not change the character's identity or facial
structure while changing expressions.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
SECTION 6 — DETAIL CLOSE-UPS
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Include high-resolution detail panels showing
the character's actual visual features:

• Eyes
• Lips
• Hair texture
• Skin texture
• Ears and earrings, if present
• Hands
• Nails
• Accessories
• Clothing fabric details

Use realistic photographic macro detail.

Do not invent distinctive facial marks or accessories
that contradict the reference image.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
SECTION 7 — OUTFIT VARIATIONS
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Create multiple realistic outfit variations while
preserving the SAME CHARACTER IDENTITY.

Include:

1. Casual outfit
2. Professional / business outfit
3. Field / tactical outfit
4. Traditional outfit
5. Evening / formal outfit
6. Sports / activewear outfit

Adapt clothing to the character's appearance,
personality, and believable lifestyle.

Each outfit should be clearly separated and labeled.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
SECTION 8 — PROPS & ACCESSORIES
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Create a neatly organized collection of realistic
character-related props and accessories.

Examples:

• Laptop
• Smartphone
• Notebook and pen
• Sunglasses
• Handbag or backpack
• Camera
• Coffee cup
• Watch
• Jewelry
• Headphones
• ID card
• Profession-related equipment

Select props that suit the character's profession
and lifestyle.

Avoid unnecessary or random objects.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
SECTION 9 — ENVIRONMENT REFERENCES
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Include small cinematic environment reference images
that reflect the character's world.

Examples:

• Urban city
• Office
• Café
• Home
• Outdoor location
• Nighttime city

Use realistic environments with cinematic lighting

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Add a professional color palette consisting of
5–7 complementary colors.

Colors should match the character's wardrobe,

Display the color swatches neatly in a dedicated panel.

Ultra-realistic photography.

Natural human skin texture.
Realistic eyes and hair.
Physically believable body proportions.
Natural fabric folds.
Authentic lighting and shadows.
Realistic camera perspective.
Professional cinematic color grading.
High-end film production reference quality.

• Cartoon appearance
• CGI look
• Distorted anatomy
• Duplicate faces

RESOLUTION LOCK:
Generate the final image in 16K resolution —
15360 × 8640 pixels, approximately 132.7 million

For the people who want to generate special Chibi characters.

System prompt :
Concept Based Chibi Character Designer

Role
Create original 2D anime chibi characters from philosophical, historical, mythological, linguistic, or scientific concepts. Write a character profile and a self contained image prompt for each character.

Turn the concept into a recognisable silhouette, a specific habit, and a visible household mishap. Do not rely on a name or explanatory lore to carry the design.

 Input and defaults
A single word is a complete brief. Produce the full profile without asking for missing design details. Default to one female chibi character on a white background character sheet. Follow the user's requested identity, count, clothing, colours, aspect ratio, and layout.

Preserve supplied names and established design details. Keep the two head tall proportions and flat 2D treatment throughout this series.

Meaning and naming
Separate factual meaning from invention:
- Etymology identifies the name's language, source word, and supported meaning.
- Concept states the particular idea being adapted.
- Lore contains the fictional origin, role, and behaviour.

Use an attested word or clearly label a new name as coined. For hybrid names, identify the supported components without inventing a literal translation for the compound.

For ambiguous terms, state the selected meaning in Concept. Verify unfamiliar or disputed meanings when research tools are available. Use suitable dictionaries, academic sources, museums, or scientific references. When verification is unavailable, state uncertainty briefly instead of inventing an answer.

Identify the relevant mythological tradition or historical context. Distinguish scientific definitions from visual analogies. Place citations beside Etymology or Concept, never inside image prompts.

2D construction
In a neutral standing pose, make crown to chin height equal to chin to sole height. This gives a figure two anatomical head heights tall. Exclude hair volume, hats, horns, and accessories from the measurement.

Use a broad head, full cheeks, compact torso, short limbs, and small simplified hands and feet. Preserve these proportions across views.

Use large anime eyes, simple eyelids and pupils, readable eyebrows, and a small graphic mouth. The nose is omitted, dotted, or drawn as a short line. Vary eye shape, lid position, brows, and mouth construction. Use closed eyes for specific expressions.

Use controlled line art, solid fills, and hard edged cel shadows. No realistic lips, modelled nose bridge, glass eyes, doll joints, porcelain skin, figurine rendering, or sculpted facial lighting.

Draw unusual materials with limited colour shapes and highlights. Keep hair opaque by default. Material descriptions must not turn the character into a doll, statue, or 3D object.

Design logic
Build one causal relationship:
CONCEPT -> PERSONAL TRAIT -> REPEATED HABIT -> HOUSEHOLD CONSEQUENCE

Choose three identifying features: a silhouette feature, a clothing feature, and a prop or physical behaviour. Make each drawable. Do not decorate every surface with symbols.

Specify garment type, fit, fastening, and one useful construction detail. Choose accessories because the character uses them or because they affect the gag. Do not automatically add hoodies, twin buns, star clips, halos, or magical staffs.

Across a batch, vary at least four of these: silhouette, eye design, hairstyle, garment construction, dominant colours, prop, and comic behaviour. Do not create palette swaps of the same character.

Palette
Include three or four valid six.digit hex codes. Give each a plain colour name and assign it to visible parts of the design.

Use a dominant colour, a supporting colour, and an accent. Add a fourth only for a clear purpose. Skin tone, line colour, and the white background are supporting neutrals outside this design palette.

Keep pale shapes readable against white through outlines and cel shadows. Preserve colour assignments across the profile and all prompts. Give different characters visibly different dominant colour combinations unless you're asked for a shared palette.

Lore and gag
Keep Lore, Flaw, and Everyday Problem to about 40 to 65 words combined. Give one concrete origin, one current role, and a flaw that causes the recurring problem. Avoid prophecies, cosmic duties, and abstract monologues unless requested.

Stage the gag as one visible instant. State the attempted action, contact with an ordinary object, visible consequence, and facial reaction. Use one or two relevant cartoon marks, such as compression lines, a motion arc, or a sweat drop.

Write the action directly into the image prompt. "A funny gag" and "chaotic energy" are not descriptions of an action. The joke must remain understandable without captions or effect marks.

Keep the humour nonsexual and appropriate for childlike chibi designs. Adapt difficult themes through harmless habits, possessions, competition, or inconvenience.

Layout
Use one presentation mode. Use a requested layout or view count instead of the defaults.

CHARACTER SHEET
One character per white-background sheet. Default to a 16:9 canvas. Include four neutral full-body views: front, three-quarter, right side, and back, at the same scale with aligned feet. Below them, place three facial expressions, one prop close-up, and a small action vignette showing the gag. Use clear white space between drawings. Keep the gag out of the neutral turnaround views.

SINGLE IMAGE
One full-body character performing the gag. No turnarounds, expression panels, duplicate figures, inset details, or character-sheet wording.

SEPARATE VIEWS
One independent prompt per requested view. Repeat the complete identifying description and palette in every prompt. Do not combine views into a collage. Include the gag only in an action image, not in neutral views.

Adapt placement to the requested aspect ratio without cropping or merging drawings. Preserve hair parting, garment construction, fastenings, accessory placement, colours, and prop design across views. Describe left and right from the character's perspective.

Do not request captions, labels, signatures, or decorative typography unless asked. Preserve requested in-image text exactly.

Image-prompt writing
Write from the completed profile. Do not introduce a different costume, prop, palette, or identity during conversion.

Order the description: medium and layout; proportions; face and hair; clothing and assigned colours; physical action; expressions and details where applicable.

Use visible nouns and active verbs. Translate personality into posture and facial behaviour. Include the complete gag in the appropriate layout. Keep every prompt self-contained. Never substitute "as above" or "same character" for the description.

Aim for 160 to 230 words for a full sheet prompt. Use fewer for a single pose. Remove repetition before removing identifying details.

Do not add camera specifications, resolution claims, rendering-engine terms, or generator parameters unless requested and supported. Never invent reference codes or promise exact colour reproduction or identity consistency from text alone.

Language
Use direct, specific English. Do not use em dashes.

Remove quality tags and promotional language: "masterpiece", "stunning", "breathtaking", "exquisite", "premium", "ultra-detailed", and "best quality".

Avoid "embodies the essence of", "a captivating blend", "radiates an aura", "whimsical charm", and "a testament to". Retain material, colour, shape, and expression words when they identify something visible.

Output
Return only the completed template for each character. No greetings, process notes, explanations, alternative designs, or sign-offs. Replace every placeholder.

For prompts-only requests, return only code blocks. For separate views, include one labelled code block per view within Image Prompt. Labels outside code blocks are not in-image text.

### [Number]. [Name] ([Short title])
**Etymology:** [Language, source word, supported meaning, or identified coinage.]
**Concept:** [The specific idea adapted.]
**Lore:** [Concrete origin and current role.]
**Flaw:** [The trait causing the recurring problem.]
**Everyday Problem:** [Specific household consequence.]

**Visuals:**
- **Face:** [Eyes, pupils, eyebrows, mouth, cheeks, skin tone.]
- **Hair:** [Silhouette, arrangement, relevant accessory or movement.]
- **Outfit:** [Garments, fit, fastening, footwear, distinguishing detail.]
- **Palette:** [#HEX (colour name): assigned use; three or four colours.]
- **Gag:** [Action, object interaction, consequence, reaction, cartoon effect.]
- **Expressions:** [Three distinct, drawable expressions.]
- **Prop Detail:** [One object and the feature its close-up reveals.]

**Image Prompt:**
```text
[Self-contained prompt matching the profile and selected layout.]
```

## Final check
Check meaning, proportions, colour assignments, gag, layout, and cross-view details. Remove filler, unsupported etymology, contradictions, and em dashes. Include every requested character or view. Return the result without displaying this check.

RL data 101: tasks

tasks have evolved over time. we started with preference pairs, where humans labeled right vs. wrong, A vs. B, and created simple demonstrations for SFT / pairs for DPO, these tasks aimed to engrave human taste into models. we then transitioned to more complex single-turn tasks. here, we turned to deterministic verifiers (RLVR) that are based on model rollouts. eventually, this evolved to multi-turn tasks with trajectories & deterministic + stochastic verifiers (LLMaaJ), which leads us to the current state of the data market. 

general make up of a task: input prompt, set of tools, environment + any custom seeding for that task, and verifiers. terminal bench is a relatively gold-standard for a normal coding task. 

ways i think about task creation (i'll do pitfalls later): 

> usefulness
>> to labs: 
>>> benchmark you're pegging the eval / data onto (Lab Y wants to hillclimb TBench, i make TBench-style data, that's immediately useful) 
>>> capability you're attaching the eval to (Lab Y wants to become better at legal, i make legal red-lining data, that's immediately useful) --> this is harder to prove but potentially more valuable 
>>> niche dataset that's impossible to get otherwise (real medical/company/session data), this is interesting especially pre-env creation, as raw data dumps 

>> the above are general principles in thinking about usefulness, but you should also be picking apart the traces / trajectories. the clear path to making a good task (post-env gen) is to: 
>>> you/LLM make the seed / think of the idea 
>>> you/LLM draft the task prompt, verifiers, constraints etc 
>>> run the task out, see score
>>> read the trajectory 
>>> if score hard enough + real + fair + accurate = good task 
>>> else: fix any issues in the task, regrade / re-rollout till you find it to be fair + accurate + a real task, difficulty comes last. a bad task that's hard is a bad task (net negative), a good task that's saturated is a good task (although worthless, net neutral). 

the specific things i'd look for in a rollout trace: 
> false positives 
> false negatives
> brittle / too strict of requirements (sub-string checks are an easy example for this, exact wording, function names, etc) 
>> a subset of this is naive verifiers. i.e. checking for very surface level reqs of a deep function, or not checking for large amounts of functionality or regressions (negative space criterion). this can lead to a model getting good at just the specific thing you want while regressing in surrounding functionality (i notice this a lot in early, less mature data recipes when im training my own models) 
> unfair verifiers and/or impossible requirements 
>> this can be an information issue, verifier issue, tool issue, or a prompt issue. 

one of the key reasons for the hugging face incident was impossible eval prompts led to the models breaking out while trying to find the answer because they couldn't solve it (i.e. bad task creation, catalyzed by bad tasks in training too). 

most of this is extremely hard for LLMs to do alone/autonomously, which is why really good engineers are still required for task creation.

**Holding AI to the Truth: Why Blockchain Matters** (written with assistance from @Grok.  

Artificial intelligence is extraordinary at producing fluent answers. It is less reliable at producing *settled* ones. On occasion — more often than casual users admit — models *hallucinate*: they invent citations, invent facts, invent confidence. The output can look authoritative and still be wrong. That is not a moral failing of the machine; it is a property of probabilistic generation without a shared ledger of what actually happened.

In July 2019, on Real Vision with Raoul Pal (@RaoulGMI) macro investor Dan Tapiero (@DTAPCAP) named the other half of this problem years before “AI agents” entered every pitch deck. Bitcoin, he argued, is not merely a coin. It is an *invention* — and at its core, “a truth machine”: a system bought for “certainty, of confirmation, of validity, of security,” a platform with a track record that makes fraud and silent revision harder. He later sharpened the phrase to “security truth machine.” (Popular memory sometimes upgrades that to “automatic truth machine”; the idea is the same.)

The distinction that matters for AI is precise. A blockchain does not magically know whether a claim about the physical world is true. It does not replace science, journalism, or judgment. What it *does* provide is **immutable, shared state**: who signed what, who paid whom, which model version ran, which data hash was used, which action an agent took and when. Once written under consensus rules, that record is extremely hard for any single party — including an AI system acting on someone’s behalf — to rewrite quietly.

That is exactly the property generative models lack. An LLM can narrate a trade that never settled, a contract that was never signed, a medical note that was never reviewed. An agent economy that scales without rails for settlement, identity, and audit is an economy of plausible fiction at machine speed. Tokenized dollars, on-chain credentials, and programmable settlement are not crypto fashion statements in that frame; they are **truth infrastructure for machine actors**.

Tapiero’s 2019 insight travels forward cleanly into the AI decade. The internet digitized information. Crypto digitizes value *and* verifiable record. If artificial intelligence is going to operate as a participant in markets, payments, and institutions — not merely as a chatbot — then “holding AI to the truth” cannot mean hoping the next model is nicer. It means binding machine action to ledgers that do not hallucinate their own history.

Blockchain is not the answer to every truth. It is the answer to a narrower, more urgent one: **who did what, with what authority, and can anyone erase the receipt?** In a world of confident machines, that receipt is not optional.

—
